history.author: Raymond Reiter
history.title: A Theory of Diagnosis from First Principles
history.scope: Conflicts of normal component assumptions generate minimal hitting set diagnoses; original theory also requires underlying system model and observations, which this proposal intentionally does NOT implement.

history.author: Johan de Kleer and Brian C Williams
history.title: Diagnosing Multiple Faults
history.scope: Early General Diagnostic Engine and minimal sets of violated assumptions applied to digital circuits; source does not promise our output ordering or certificate serialization.

original_vs_ours: Reiter supplies the correspondence minimal conflicts ↔ subset-minimal hitting sets; returning deterministic canonical order, original-index private conflict certificates, input type errors, and explicit empty-family/empty-conflict distinctions are additional SENS research contracts, not historical APIs.

candidate.arguments: (finite ordered tuple of distinct, nonempty exact component IDs; finite ordered tuple of finite component-set conflicts, all IDs from universe). Components are abstract exact identities, NOT English runtime identifiers or hardware coordinates.
candidate.result: If any conflict is empty: NO-DIAGNOSIS with earliest empty-conflict index. Else: DIAGNOSES of ALL inclusion-minimal hitting sets, each ordered by input-universe position, result tuples lexicographically ordered by input positions. For every chosen component c return earliest original conflict whose intersection with that hitting set is exactly {c}, proving subset-minimality.
candidate.law: H subset U hits every conflict C_i when H ∩ C_i != ∅. H is inclusion-minimal iff each h∈H has a private original conflict C_i with H ∩ C_i={h}. Do NOT substitute smallest cardinality, probability rankings or one arbitrary diagnosis. No conflicts => exactly one empty diagnosis. Any empty conflict => NO-DIAGNOSIS even for nonempty U. Superset/repeated conflicts preserve semantic result and original witness indices.

sample_cases.explanation: {b} and {a,c} both inclusion-minimal; a single cardinality-optimal {b} is insufficient
no conflict: empty hitting set is unique subset-minimal diagnosis
redundant superset conflict doesn't add diagnoses

falsifiers: Returning only {b} for conflicts {a,b},{b,c} misses valid subset-minimal {a,c}.
Returning {a,b} when {b} hits all conflicts is not subset-minimal.
Returning NO-DIAGNOSES for zero conflicts is wrong: exactly one empty diagnosis exists.
Ignoring a single empty conflict and returning diagnoses is unsound.
A certificate citing a conflict also hit by another selected component is not a private-conflict proof.
Using diagnosis cardinality as the tie criterion instead of inclusion-minimality drops incomparable diagnoses.
Hard-wiring English component names rather than using ordered opaque input IDs would violate binary-first identity.
Accepting conflict components outside universe or repeated universe identifiers without error invents assumptions.

candidate.precise_scope: The caller must supply a complete relevant conflict family. This operation does NOT infer conflict sets from a system model, prove real-world component failure, propose a measurement, or choose a repair. Output candidates are algebraic diagnoses conditional on input conflicts.
owner_hobby_fanout: Radio/TV/electronics repair: competing minimal fault combinations in digital or analog circuits
FPGA and ESP32: violated device-assumption sets in gate and sensor validation
SDR/horology: contradictions among clock/signal diagnostic assumptions
WSM-OS-Lisp/SENS: minimal dependency changes after proof/CI failures
Advice Taker, Prolog, Panini: logical assumptions behind mutually contradictory derived conclusions
Astronomy/physics: candidate instrument/model assumptions explaining incompatible observations
candidate.derivability: Finite hypergraph transversal enumeration is constructible from finite lists, subset/intersection, recursion and comparison; no proof that this must be irreducible D10 core; owner must review whether an explicit useful reusable function warrants research selection.
